newsitem.title: USA: Fast reporting called critical in child abductions.
newsitem.headline: Fast reporting called critical in child abductions.

text.p: Quick reporting of missing children is vital to avoid tragedy, a study of child kidnappings and murders released Tuesday said.
The study, conducted for the U.S. Justice Department by Washington state officials, looked at more than 600 child abduction and death records from 44 states.

In 60 percent of the cases studied, there was a delay of more than two hours between the time the victim was known to be missing and when police were notified. In 74 percent of the cases, the victim was dead within three hours of being snatched.
"If you have a 6- or 8-year-old missing, the police want to know right away," said study author Robert Keppel, chief criminal investigator for the Washington attorney general's office.
He said the study also pointed to the need for immediate action by police on receipt of a missing child report.

The report said in almost two-thirds of cases, the abductions were "snatch and grab" confrontations where the predator saw an available victim, then quickly assaulted and subdued him or her. In 53 percent of cases, victim and abductor were strangers to each other.
Even though child abduction-murder cases are extremely rare, averaging 100 per year in the United States, Keppel said it paid for parents to be vigilant.
In well over half the cases reviewed, the initial contact site was within a quarter-mile of the victim's home.
